families.title: Pebble Duel: stalks
families.mathematics: Stalks of blue and red segments stand on the ground. Blue cuts one blue segment, Red one red segment, and everything above a cut falls off; whoever has nothing to cut loses. Every board is a number, and the numbers of boards side by side add: B is 1, R is −1, and in a stalk the first run of one colour counts one each, after which each segment counts half the one below it, so BR is 1/2, BRR is 1/4, BRB is 3/4 and RB is −1/2. Blue wins whoever starts when the number is positive, Red when it is negative, and whoever moves second when it is zero: a zero board balances. No board is won by whoever moves first. So two BR balance R, two BRR balance RB, and any stalk balances its colour swap, since the second player can copy every cut with colours swapped.
rules: Blue cuts one blue segment; Red cuts one red segment. Everything above a cut falls off.
Players take turns. Whoever has nothing to cut loses.
A board balances when whoever goes second can always win, whichever colour starts. The app never misses a winning cut.

puzzles.title: BB and R
puzzles.objective: Leave me nothing to cut. You go first.
puzzles.instruction: Leave me nothing to cut. You go first.
puzzles.controls: Blue cuts one blue segment and Red one red segment; everything above a cut falls off. Whoever has nothing to cut loses. You are Blue, and you go first. Tap one of your segments to cut it. I reply at once. Undo takes back your cut and my reply.
rules: Blue cuts one blue segment; Red cuts one red segment.
Everything above a cut falls off.
Players take turns. Whoever has nothing to cut loses.

You are Blue and go first.
puzzles.idea: A low cut drops your own segments too. As Blue first on BB and R, cut the top B, not the bottom one.
puzzles.prerequisites: None. A grown-up can read how a cut works.
hints: Which of your two segments would you rather keep?
If you cut the bottom B, the top one falls too. What can you cut after that?
Cut the top B.

parent.notice: Whether your child sees that cutting the bottom segment drops the one above it, and after a loss tries the other cut.
parent.prompt: Why does cutting the bottom B lose?
parent.explanation: Blue has two cuts. The bottom B drops both blue segments and leaves R: I cut it, and Blue has nothing left. The top B leaves B and R: I must cut R, and Blue cuts the last B, leaving me nothing. A low cut costs everything above it, your own segments included.
parent.extension: If Red starts on BB and R, who wins?
parent.connection: Red–blue Hackenbush is a partizan game: Blue and Red have different moves. Conway showed that every board is a number, that boards side by side add, and that a board is won by whoever moves second exactly when its number is zero (Winning Ways, Chapters 1–2). A stalk’s number comes from its colours by sign expansion: the first run of one colour counts whole units, and each later segment half the one below it.

puzzles.provenance: Week 83 Problem 1, board D (BB and R, where cutting low costs Blue its own top segment), as a duel against a perfect opponent with Blue first, as the card’s App fit asks.

parent.notice: Whether your child chooses by looking at the board, and notices on B and R that whoever cuts first loses.
parent.prompt: On which boards can one colour always win? On which does the second player win?
parent.explanation: On B, Blue wins whoever starts, since Red has nothing to cut; R is the same for Red. On B and R whoever moves first must cut their only segment, and then the other cuts theirs: the second player wins. On BB and R Blue wins whoever starts, provided Blue, moving first, cuts the top B. Choosing a colour lets me choose who starts, so it wins only when that colour wins both ways; Me second lets me choose my colour and go first, so it wins only when the second player always wins.
parent.extension: Can you find a board where whoever goes first always wins, whichever colour starts? (There is none in this game.)

puzzles.objective: Leave me nothing to cut. You go first.

puzzles.idea: As Red first on BR and R, cut the R on top of BR, leaving B and R for Blue to start; cutting the lone R leaves BR, which Blue wins.

parent.notice: Whether your child aims for a board they know, B and R, rather than cutting the lone R because it stands alone.
parent.prompt: Is BR worth as much to Blue as B?
parent.explanation: Red has two cuts. The lone R leaves BR: Blue cuts its B, everything falls, and Red has nothing. The R on top of BR leaves B and R with Blue to move, and whoever moves first there loses. If Blue started instead, Blue’s only cut removes the whole BR and Red cuts R. So BR and R is Red’s whoever starts: BR is worth less than a B (it is 1/2).
parent.extension: Who wins BR, BR and R?

Conway showed that every board is a number, that boards side by side add, and that a board is won by whoever moves second exactly when its number is zero (Winning Ways, Chapters 1–2). A stalk’s number comes from its colours by sign expansion: the first run of one colour counts whole units, and each later segment half the one below it.

parent.notice: Whether your child answers each first cut by aiming for a known board, B and R, and sees that the reply depends on which colour cut.
parent.prompt: Why does whoever goes second win here, whichever colour starts?
parent.explanation: BR, BR and R is a second-player win, which the worksheet calls a balance: two BR count for Blue exactly as much as one R for Red, so a BR is worth half a B. Up to swapping the two BR there are three first cuts. If Blue removes a BR, Red cuts the top of the other, leaving B and R with Blue to move. If Red cuts the top of a BR, Blue removes the other BR, leaving B and R with Red to move. If Red cuts the lone R, Blue removes either BR, leaving one BR, which Blue wins.
parent.extension: Does BR, BR, BR and R balance?
parent.connection: Red–blue Hackenbush is a partizan game: Blue and Red have different moves. Conway showed that every board is a number, that boards side by side add, and that a board is won by whoever moves second exactly when its number is zero (Winning Ways, Chapters 1–2). A stalk’s number comes from its colours by sign expansion: the first run of one colour counts whole units, and each later segment half the one below it.

puzzles.title: BRR and RB
puzzles.objective: Leave me nothing to cut. You go first.
puzzles.instruction: Leave me nothing to cut. You go first.

parent.notice: Whether your child compares BR with RB, a stalk with its colours swapped.
parent.prompt: Why do BR and RB balance?
parent.explanation: BRR and RB is Red’s whoever starts (1/4 − 1/2 < 0). Red, first, has three cuts. The top R of BRR leaves BR and RB: whatever one player cuts on one stalk, the other cuts on the other stalk with colours swapped, so the second player wins (1/2 − 1/2 = 0). The middle R of BRR leaves B and RB (1 − 1/2 > 0), and the R under RB removes that stalk and leaves BRR (1/4 > 0): Blue wins both.
parent.extension: Does BRR, BRR and RB balance?
parent.connection: Red–blue Hackenbush is a partizan game: Blue and Red have different moves. Conway showed that every board is a number, that boards side by side add, and that a board is won by whoever moves second exactly when its number is zero (Winning Ways, Chapters 1–2). A stalk’s number comes from its colours by sign expansion: the first run of one colour counts whole units, and each later segment half the one below it.

puzzles.provenance: Week 83 Problem 3, board A (BRR against RB, Red’s whoever starts), as a duel with Red first, as the card’s App fit asks.

puzzles.title: Balance BRB
puzzles.objective: Add stalks so that whoever goes second can always win, whichever colour starts. Then press Check.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Add stalks so the second player can always win, whichever colour starts.

puzzles.controls: Blue cuts one blue segment and Red one red segment; everything above a cut falls off. Whoever has nothing to cut loses. Tap + to add a blue or red segment to a spot, and tap a segment you added to take it off with everything above it. Check tests the whole board. If whoever goes second can always win, whichever colour starts, it balances and you are done. If not, I take the colour that can win going first, go first and win; then Back returns to your board, and Check waits for a change.

puzzles.idea: RBR, the colour swap, balances BRB; so do R with BRR, and RB with RBB.
hints: Which boards that balance do you know? What makes them balance?
In BR and RB, one stalk is the other with its colours swapped.
Build RBR in one spot.

parent.notice: Whether your child copies the stalk with its colours swapped, and whether, after a Check that fails, they use the game I played to change the board.
parent.prompt: How do you know your board balances?
parent.explanation: A board balances when its number is zero. BRB is 1 − 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4, so the spots must add up to −3/4. RBR is −3/4: any stalk balances its colour swap, since the second player copies every cut on the other stalk with colours swapped. So are R and BRR (−1 + 1/4), and RB and RBB (−1/2 − 1/4). Check decides by searching the game, not by the numbers; a failed Check is played out by me in the colour that wins going first.
parent.extension: Can you balance BRB with two stalks, neither of them RBR?
parent.connection: Red–blue Hackenbush is a partizan game: Blue and Red have different moves. Conway showed that every board is a number, that boards side by side add, and that a board is won by whoever moves second exactly when its number is zero (Winning Ways, Chapters 1–2). A stalk’s number comes from its colours by sign expansion: the first run of one colour counts whole units, and each later segment half the one below it.

parent.notice: Whether your child reuses BR and RB as a known balance, and finds replies that leave a board my colour cannot win.
parent.prompt: Why does whoever goes second win here?
parent.explanation: BRR is 1/4 and RB is −1/2, so two BRR and RB add up to 0: whoever goes second wins. The five first cuts and winning replies: Blue removes a BRR, and Red cuts the top R of the other, leaving BR and RB. Blue cuts the B of RB, and Red cuts the top R of a BRR, leaving BR, BRR and R (−1/4 with Blue to move). Red cuts the middle R of a BRR, and Blue removes the other BRR (B and RB) or cuts the B of RB. Red cuts the top R of a BRR, and Blue removes the other BRR, leaving BR and RB. Red removes RB, and Blue removes a BRR, leaving one BRR.
parent.extension: Does BRR, BRR, BRR and RB balance?
parent.connection: Red–blue Hackenbush is a partizan game: Blue and Red have different moves. Conway showed that every board is a number, that boards side by side add, and that a board is won by whoever moves second exactly when its number is zero (Winning Ways, Chapters 1–2). A stalk’s number comes from its colours by sign expansion: the first run of one colour counts whole units, and each later segment half the one below it.

parent.prompt: How do you decide what to choose?
parent.explanation: Blue wins whoever starts when the board’s number is positive, Red when it is negative, and whoever goes second when it is zero. A colour lets me choose who starts, so it wins only when that colour wins both ways; Me second lets me choose my colour and go first, so it wins only on a zero board; no board is a first-player win, so one choice always wins. Boards are drawn from every set of 2 to 4 stalks from B, R, BB, RR, BR, RB, BRR, RBB, BRB and RBR with 3 to 8 segments, both colours and a stalk of both colours; each draw is Blue’s, Red’s or balanced with equal chance, and the app never misses a win, so three wins in a row from new boards shows the choice is known, not guessed.
parent.extension: Make a board of three stalks that balances, with no stalk the colour swap of another.

Conway showed that every board is a number, that boards side by side add, and that a board is won by whoever moves second exactly when its number is zero (Winning Ways, Chapters 1–2). A stalk’s number comes from its colours by sign expansion: the first run of one colour counts whole units, and each later segment half the one below it.
